AND AWARD DATED 31ST DAY OF OCTOBER 2022 PASSED BY THE II ADDL. JUDGE & ACMM,
COURT OF SMALL CAUSES, MACT-13 BENGALURU, IN MVC NO.4151/2019 AND ENHANCE COMPENSATION FROM RS.16,33,753/- TO RS.1,00,00,000/- WITH COST AND INTEREST, IN THE INTEREST OF JUSTICE AND EQUITY.
THIS APPEAL, COMING ON FOR FURTHER HEARING, THIS DAY, JUDGMENT WAS DELIVERED THEREIN AS UNDER:
CORAM: HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE K.S.MUDAGAL  and  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAYKUMAR A. PATIL
ORAL JUDGMENT AND ORDER ON I.A.NO.1/2024 (PER: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAYKUMAR A. PATIL)
Challenging the judgment and award in MVC No.4151/2019 passed by the MACT, Bengaluru (SCCH-13), injured - claimant has filed this appeal.
2. The appellant was the claimant and respondents Nos.1 and 2 were respondent Nos.1 and 2 before the Tribunal.
For the purpose of convenience, the parties are referred to henceforth according to their ranks before the Tribunal.

The injured - claimant filed claim petition under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988,
seeking compensation of Rs.1,00,00,000/- for the injuries sustained by him in a road traffic accident that occurred on 26.06.2019.

It was pleaded that when claimant was proceeding in a motorcycle bearing registration No.TN-70 J-8011 on Hosur road, the rider of another motorcycle bearing registration No.TN-70 V-6390 came from opposite direction in a rash and negligent manner, dashed the motorcycle of the claimant due to which the claimant fell down and sustained grievous injuries.
It was further pleaded that the claimant was initially provided treatment at local hospital, Hosur, then shifted to Vaidehi Hospital, Bengaluru wherein he underwent surgery.
It was also pleaded that the claimant was aged about 29 years, working as a Welder and earning Rs.30,000/- p.m.

Due to the injuries suffered in the road accident, he became permanently disabled Ravikumar Narayana Reddy vs Aravindh S on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/184646468/
2 and lost his earning.

sentences.text: Hence, he filed the claim petition seeking compensation.
4. Respondent No.1 did not appear before the Tribunal and was placed exparte.
Respondent No.2 denied the NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB averments made in the claim petition.
It was pleaded that the offending vehicle was insured with it.
However, the liability is subject to fulfillment of conditions of the policy and requirement of law.
It was further pleaded that claimant without noticing the vehicle coming from opposite direction, negligently turned the vehicle which resulted in the accident.
It was also pleaded that the claim of compensation by the claimant was exorbitant and without any basis.
Hence, sought for dismissal of the claim petition.
5. The Tribunal recorded the evidence of the parties.
Claimant examined himself as PW-1, other witnesses as PWs-2 to 5 and got marked Exs.P1 to P30.
The respondents examined RW-1 but did not produce any documentary evidence.
Medical Board report was marked as Ex-C1.
The Tribunal, on appreciation of the pleading and evidence on record, partly allowed the claim petition holding that accident occurred due to culpable negligence of respondent No.1.

The Tribunal further recorded the finding that the claimant suffered 50% permanent disability, assessed his income at Rs.14,000/-
p.m. and awarded compensation of Rs.14,28,000/- under the head of loss of future earnings and in total, awarded compensation of NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB Rs.16,33,753/- with interest @ 6% p.a.
from the date of petition till deposit.
The claimant is in appeal seeking higher compensation.
6. Sri
.A.Srinivasaiah, learned counsel for the appellant submits that the Tribunal committed grave error in assessing the income as well as the disability of the claimant on lower side.
It is submitted that the claimant was working as a Welder and earning Rs.30,000/- p.m.
Without appreciating the same, the Tribunal assessed his income at Rs.14,000/- p.m. which is on the lower side.
It is further submitted that the Tribunal assessed the disability at 50% which is contrary to the evidence of PWs-3 to 5 and Ex.C1.
It is also submitted that the Tribunal did not consider the fact that the claimant has lost his vision and he would not be in a position to do his avocation of welding.

Hence,
the functional disability of claimant has to be considered at 100% and future prospects on earnings also to be awarded.
It is pleaded that the award of compensation under the heads of pain and suffering, loss of amenities, future medical expenses and other conventional heads are also on the lower side.

Hence, he seeks to enhance the compensation appropriately under the aforesaid heads.
NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB 7.

Per contra, Sri.Ravi S.Samprathi, learned counsel for respondent No.2 supports the impugned judgment and award of the Tribunal and submits that the claimant has not produced any evidence with regard to the income.
Hence, the Tribunal has rightly assessed his income notionally at Rs.14,000/- p.m. which does not call for any modification.

It is submitted that the Tribunal has referred the claimant to Victoria Hospital wherein the Medical Board has re-assessed the disability of the claimant and sent the report marked as Ex.C1 which indicates that the claimant has suffered orthopedic disability to the extent of 31% and neurological disability to the extent of 48%.

It is further submitted that the orthopedic disability is not to the whole body and if 1/3rd of the orthopedic disability is taken into consideration, then the whole body disability of the claimant can be assessed at maximum 60%.

It is also submitted that the Tribunal, on the available evidence, has Ravikumar Narayana Reddy vs Aravindh S on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/184646468/
3 awarded just compensation to the claimant which does not call for any enhancement.

sentences.text: Hence, he seeks dismissal of the appeal.

Considering the rival submissions of the parties and examining the materials on records, the point that arises for consideration is "Whether the impugned judgment and award of the Tribunal calls for any interference"?
ANALYSIS 9.

The undisputed facts are that in a road accident that occurred on 26.06.2019 the claimant suffered disability to the extent of 42% to the particular limb and 48% permanent disability to the whole body as per the assessment by PWs-3 and 4.
It is also not in dispute that respondent No.1 was negligent and caused the accident in question.
Respondent No.2 has insured the vehicle in question.
Hence, the Tribunal saddled the liability on respondent No.2 to pay the compensation.
The Tribunal assessed the income of the claimant at Rs.14,000/- p.m. as the claimant failed to produce any legally acceptable evidence.
Insofar as assessment of income by the Tribunal, the same is based on pleadings and evidence on record which does not call for any modification.
10. Before adverting to disability of the appellant, it would be useful to refer to the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB in the case of Rajkumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Another1,
wherein relevant paragraphs read thus:

"11. What requires to be assessed by the Tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured; and after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of a percentage of the income, it has to be quantified in terns of money, to arrive at the future loss of earnings (by applying the standard multiplier method used to determine loss of dependency).

We may however note that in some cases, on appreciation of evidence and assessment, the Tribunal may find that percentage of loss of earning capacity as a result of the permanent disability, is approximately the same as the percentage of permanent disability in which case, of course, the Tribunal will adopt the said percentage for determination of compensation.
13.
Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood.

sentences.text: For example, if the left hand of a claimant is amputated, the permanent physical or functional disablement may be assessed around 60%.

If the (2011) 1 SCC 343 NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB claimant was a driver or a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be hundred percent, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry.

On the other hand, if the claimant was a clerk in government service, the loss of his left hand may not result in loss of employment and he may still be continued as a clerk as he could perform his clerical functions; and in that event the loss of earning capacity will not be 100% as in the case of a driver or carpenter, nor 60% which is the actual physical disability, but far less.

In fact, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of `loss of future earnings', if the claimant continues in government service, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities as a consequence of losing his hand.

Sometimes the injured claimant may be continued in service, but may not found suitable for discharging the duties attached to the post or job which he was earlier holding, on account of his disability, and may therefore be shifted to some other suitable but lesser post with lesser emoluments, in which case there should be a limited award under the head of loss of future earning capacity, taking note of the reduced earning capacity."
(Emphasis supplied)
11.

In another decision, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Laxman Vs. Oriental Insurance Company Limited , at paragraph-15 of the judgment has held as under:
"15.

The ratio of the above noted judgments is that if the victim of an accident suffers permanent or temporary disability, then efforts should always be made to award adequate compensation not only for physical injury and treatment, but also for the pain, suffering and trauma caused due to the accident, loss of earnings and victim's inability to lead a normal life and enjoy amenities, which he would have enjoyed but for the disability caused due to the accident."
(2011) 10 SCC 756 - 10 - NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB (Emphasis supplied)
12.

It is apt and necessary to refer the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Jagdish Vs.
Mohan & Others3, wherein at paragraph-14 is observed as under:
14.
In making the computation in the present case, the Court must be mindful of the fact that the appellant has suffered a serious disability in which he has suffered a loss of the use of both his hands.
For a person engage in manual activities, it requires no stretch of imagination to understand that a loss of hands is a complete deprivation of the ability to earn.

5 atleast in the facts of this case- can restore lost hands.

sentences.text: But the measure of compensation must reflect a genuine attempt of the law to restore the dignity of the being.
Our yardsticks of compensation should not be so abysmal as to lead one to question whether our law values human life.
If it does, as it must, it must provide a realistic recompense for the pain of loss and the trauma of suffering.
Awards of compensation are not law's doles.
In a discourse of rights, they constitute entitlements under law.
Our conversations about law must shift from a paternalistic subordination of the individual to an assertion of enforceable rights as intrinsic to human dignity.
(Emphasis supplied)

13. In a recent decision, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sarnam Singh vs. Shriram General Insurance Co. Ltd. and Others4, has held as under:
"9. As to how compensation, in case where permanent disability of an injured affects his functional disability, is to be assessed has been considered by this Court,
repeatedly.

Reference can be made to the judgment of this Court in Mohan Soni vs.
Ram Avtar (2018) 4 SCC 571 2023 LiveLaw (SC) 498 - 11 - NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB Tomar And Others.

sentences.text: In the aforesaid case the injured was working as a cart puller.
As a result of the accident, his left leg was amputated.
His permanent disability was assessed at 60%.
The Tribunal assessed the compensation taking the loss of earning at 50% on the theory that he can still do some other work while sitting.
The High Court did not disturb the finding regarding loss of income on account of disability.
This Court found that the Tribunal was in error in taking the loss of earning at 50% as the injured was 55 years of age and it may be difficult for him to find a job at that stage.
In fact, any physical disability resulting from an accident has to be judged with reference to the nature of the work being performed by the person who suffered disability.
The same injury suffered by two different persons may affect them in different ways.
Loss of leg by a farmer or a rickshaw puller may be end of the road as far as his earning capacity is concerned.
Whereas, in case of the persons engaged in some kind of desk work in office, loss of leg may have lesser effect.
This Court enhanced the loss of earning capacity from 50% to 90%."

(Emphasis supplied)
14. Keeping in mind the aforesaid enunciation of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court,
insofar as disability of the claimant is concerned, the evidence available on record indicate that immediately after the accident the claimant was provided treatment at local hospital, Hosur and thereafter was shifted to Vaidehi Hospital, Bengaluru.

sentences.text: 3. Fracture of left femur bone - 12 - NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB 15.
The claimant got examined himself as PW-1 and deposed with regard to the income, avocation and disability suffered by him.
The claimant has examined PW-3 Dr.S.A.Somashekar, an Orthopedic Surgeon.
The evidence of PW-3 indicates that he examined the claimant on 30.09.2021 for the purpose of assessment of disability.
It is observed by the said doctor that the claimant was diagnosed with head injury and displaced fracture of shaft of left femur.
He further observed that the claimant underwent surgery in the form of CRIF with IMIL nailing on 05.07.2019 which means the claimant underwent surgery to fix bones and nails have been inserted.
The said witness states that the claimant has walking difficulty.

He has assessed the total disability of left lower limb at 42%
and that of his whole body at 21%.
He further observed that the said disability would come in the way of working as Welder and he needs surgery for removal of implant which would cost Rs.30,000/- in private set up.
The claimant is entitled to a sum of Rs.30,000/- under the head of future medical expenses.
The said witness has been cross-examined, however nothing has been elicited which would help the Insurance Company.
The claimant has also examined Dr.B.G.Srihari, Neurosurgeon as PW-4.
His evidence indicates that he is not a treated doctor.
However, he has examined the claimant and assessed the disability.
He has deposed that the claimant complaints head ache from last two years, has loss of vision of left eye as also loss of memory and aggressive behaviour.
He further observed that the claimant has higher mental function deficit and third nerve palsy.

He has advised further MRI brain plan,
Neuro-Psychologist opinion and Ophthalmologist opinion.
He assessed neurological whole body disability at 48% and advised for Neuro-rehabilitation.
The said witness has been cross-examined.

In the cross-examination, he has clearly rejected the suggestion that the claimant can perform his day- to-day activities normally without any difficulties, also denied the suggestion that there is no difficulty in pronouncing the words and speech disorder.
17. The claimant has examined Dr.Krishna Prasad A.H., Ophthalmologist.
He has examined the claimant on 30.09.2021 and is of the opinion that the claimant has lost vision of left eye and is unable to perform the day-to-day work.
However, he - 14 - NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB has not assessed any specific disability with regard to the vision of left eye.
In the cross-examination, he has denied the suggestion that the movement of left eye is improved by 80% to 90%.

The Tribunal has referred the claimant to Victoria Hospital for the Ravikumar Narayana Reddy vs Aravindh S on 11 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/184646468/
7 purpose of assessment of disability.

sentences.text: The report of Victoria Hospital is marked as Ex.C1.
The said report indicates that the claimant has been examined by three expert doctors and disability is assessed to an extent of 31% to the orthopedic and to an extent of 48% to neurological.

On appreciation of the pleadings and the oral testimony of PWs-3 to 5 and Ex.C1, it is evident that the disability assessed by the Orthopedic Surgeon was 42% to the left lower limb and 21% to the whole body.
However, subsequently the experts at Victoria Hospital have assessed orthopedic disability at 31%.
It is not forthcoming from Ex.C1 whether the disability assessed by the Medical Board is to a particular limb or to the whole body.

Considering the oral testimony of PW-3 and Ex.C1, we are of the considered view that the claimant's orthopedic disability to the whole body assessed at 25%
would meet the ends of justice.
Insofar as Neurological disability of the claimant is concerned, PW-4 has assessed the disability at 48% to the whole body and has assigned reasons for arriving at such conclusion.
The said assessment of disability is further corroborated with Ex.C1 - the disability assessed by the Medical Board.
The Medical Board of Victoria Hospital has also assessed the Neurological disability of the claimant at 48%.
Hence, we have no reason to disbelieve the evidence of PW-4 and Ex.C1.
Hence, we consider the Neurological disability of the claimant to the whole body at 48%.
The evidence of PW-5 clearly indicates that the claimant has substantially lost the vision of the left eye.

Considering the oral testimony of PWs-4 and 5 who have also spoken with regard to the loss of vision of left eye of the claimant, we assess the disability for the purpose of assessment of compensation for the left eye at 20%.

The evidence of PWs-2 to 5 clearly indicate that the claimant would not be in a position to continue his avocation of welding which he was doing prior to the accident as per the pleadings and evidence available on record.

Having assessed the Orthopedic disability of the claimant at 25% to the whole body, 48% Neurological disability to the whole body and 20% to the left - 16 - NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB eye, we are of the view that the claimant would not be in a position to continue his avocation what he was doing prior to the accident.

Hence, considering the disability assessed supra, we are of the considered view that the interest of justice would be met if we re-assess the functional disability at 80% for the purpose of determination of the compensation.
19. We have recorded the finding with regard to the income of the claimant supra.

Having assessed the income of the claimant at Rs.14,000/- p.m. and functional disability at 80% for the purpose of determination of compensation, we are of the considered view that the claimant is also entitled to compensation on the head of loss of future prospects at 40% of the assessed income as per the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in National Insurance Company Limited Vs. Pranay Sethi & Others5.

Considering the rival submissions of the parties and examining the materials on records, the point that arises for consideration is "Whether the impugned judgment and award of the Tribunal calls for any interference"?
ANALYSIS 9.
The undisputed facts are that in a road accident that occurred on 26.06.2019 the claimant suffered disability to the extent of 42% to the particular limb and 48% permanent disability to the whole body as per the assessment by PWs-3 and 4.
wherein relevant paragraphs read thus:
"11. What requires to be assessed by the Tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured; and after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of a percentage of the income, it has to be quantified in terns of money, to arrive at the future loss of earnings (by applying the standard multiplier method used to determine loss of dependency).
We may however note that in some cases, on appreciation of evidence and assessment, the Tribunal may find that percentage of loss of earning capacity as a result of the permanent disability, is approximately the same as the percentage of permanent disability in which case, of course, the Tribunal will adopt the said percentage for determination of compensation.
13.
Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.
The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood.

In making the computation in the present case, the Court must be mindful of the fact that the appellant has suffered a serious disability in which he has suffered a loss of the use of both his hands.
But the measure of compensation must reflect a genuine attempt of the law to restore the dignity of the being.
Our yardsticks of compensation should not be so abysmal as to lead one to question whether our law values human life.
If it does, as it must, it must provide a realistic recompense for the pain of loss and the trauma of suffering.
Awards of compensation are not law's doles.
In a discourse of rights, they constitute entitlements under law.
13. In a recent decision, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sarnam Singh vs. Shriram General Insurance Co. Ltd. and Others4, has held as under:

repeatedly.

The evidence of PWs-2 to 5 clearly indicate that the claimant would not be in a position to continue his avocation of welding which he was doing prior to the accident as per the pleadings and evidence available on record.
Having assessed the Orthopedic disability of the claimant at 25% to the whole body, 48% Neurological disability to the whole body and 20% to the left - 16 - NC: 2024:KHC:45633-DB eye, we are of the view that the claimant would not be in a position to continue his avocation what he was doing prior to the accident.
Having assessed the income of the claimant at Rs.14,000/- p.m. and functional disability at 80% for the purpose of determination of compensation, we are of the considered view that the claimant is also entitled to compensation on the head of loss of future prospects at 40% of the assessed income as per the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in National Insurance Company Limited Vs. Pranay Sethi & Others5.
